subject: ela
intro: Read each embedded passage carefully. Trace the author's argument and evaluate the claims: figure out what the author wants you to believe, which parts are claims, which are reasons or evidence, and whether the support is strong enough. Choose the single best answer.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Our town should build a new public library. The old library is too small to hold the books people want. Last year, more than 400 residents had to wait weeks for books because the shelves were full. A bigger building would let the library keep more titles and serve more readers. A new library would make our whole community stronger.

What is the author's main argument in this passage?

A) The old library is a popular place that many people visit.
B) Our town should build a new public library.
C) Last year more than 400 residents waited weeks for books.
D) Libraries hold books that people want to read.
items.answer: B) Our town should build a new public library.

steps: The main argument is the position the author wants the reader to accept, and the passage opens and closes by urging the town to build a new library, so B is correct.
A names a detail about the old library, not the position the author is arguing for.
C is a piece of evidence the author uses to support the argument, not the argument itself.
D states the general topic of libraries rather than the specific position the author takes, which is the topic-versus-argument mix-up.
solution.answer: B) Our town should build a new public library.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Schools should start later in the morning. Teenagers naturally fall asleep late, so early start times leave them exhausted. A study of three high schools found that students who started class at 8:30 instead of 7:30 scored higher on tests. Well rested students learn better. Later start times would help students succeed.

Which sentence states a claim the author is trying to prove?

A) A study of three high schools found that students who started class at 8:30 instead of 7:30 scored higher on tests.
B) Schools should start later in the morning.
C) Teenagers naturally fall asleep late.
D) The study looked at three high schools.
items.answer: B) Schools should start later in the morning.

steps: A claim is a statement the author wants the reader to accept and that needs support, and 'Schools should start later in the morning' is exactly the position the author argues for, so B is correct.
A reports the study results, which is evidence offered to back the claim, not the claim itself.
C is a reason the author gives, but the central claim the author is trying to prove is the call to start school later.
D is a minor factual detail about the study and is not a claim the author is arguing for.
solution.answer: B) Schools should start later in the morning.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Communities should plant more trees along city streets. Trees cool the air on hot days, which lowers the temperature for everyone walking by. In one city, streets lined with trees were measured at 10 degrees cooler than streets with no trees. Trees also clean the air and make neighborhoods look better.

Which sentence is evidence the author uses, not a claim?

A) Communities should plant more trees along city streets.
B) Trees also make neighborhoods look better.
C) In one city, streets lined with trees were measured at 10 degrees cooler than streets with no trees.
D) Trees cool the air on hot days.
items.answer: C) In one city, streets lined with trees were measured at 10 degrees cooler than streets with no trees.

steps: Evidence is concrete proof such as a fact, measurement, or statistic, and the 10 degree measurement is a specific fact offered to prove the point, so C is correct.
A is the author's overall claim, the position the reader is asked to accept.
B is an opinion-style claim about appearance, not measured proof.
D is a claim about what trees do, which the measurement in C is meant to support, so it is the claim, not the evidence.
solution.answer: C) In one city, streets lined with trees were measured at 10 degrees cooler than streets with no trees.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Our school should keep its daily recess. First, recess gives students a break that helps them focus. A teacher survey found that after recess, students completed 20 percent more classwork than on days when recess was canceled. Second, recess is the best part of the school day. Everybody knows that kids love to run around outside, and taking that away would be terrible. Recess clearly belongs in our schedule.

Which claim does the author make without backing it up with reasons or evidence?

A) Recess gives students a break that helps them focus.
B) After recess, students completed 20 percent more classwork.
C) Recess is the best part of the school day.
D) Students should have a daily recess.
items.answer: C) Recess is the best part of the school day.

steps: An unsupported claim rests on opinion or feeling with no reasons or evidence behind it, and 'recess is the best part of the school day' is backed only by the emotional line that kids love it, so C is correct.
A is supported by the survey result that follows it, so it is not unsupported.
B is itself the evidence (a statistic), not an unsupported claim.
D is the overall position, which the author does support with the focus and classwork evidence, so it is not the unsupported claim.
solution.answer: C) Recess is the best part of the school day.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The city should add a bike lane on Main Street. Many people would ride bikes if the street felt safe. A traffic count showed that 1,200 cars use Main Street each day, while only 30 bikes do, even though a nearby park draws hundreds of cyclists on weekends. A protected lane would separate riders from cars and encourage more people to bike to work. Safer streets mean a healthier city.

Which detail does the author use to support the claim that more people would bike if the street felt safe?

A) Safer streets mean a healthier city.
B) A nearby park draws hundreds of cyclists on weekends, but only 30 bikes use Main Street each day.
C) 1,200 cars use Main Street each day.
D) A protected lane would separate riders from cars.
items.answer: B) A nearby park draws hundreds of cyclists on weekends, but only 30 bikes use Main Street each day.

steps: The claim is that more people would bike if the street felt safe, and the contrast between hundreds of cyclists at a safe park and only 30 on busy Main Street is the evidence that the gap is about safety, so B is correct.
A is a broad concluding claim, not evidence for the specific point about safety.
C is a true detail from the passage but it counts cars, which does not directly show that riders are held back by feeling unsafe, so it is an irrelevant match.
D describes what the lane would do, which is part of the proposal rather than evidence that people would ride if it felt safe.
solution.answer: B) A nearby park draws hundreds of cyclists on weekends, but only 30 bikes use Main Street each day.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Students should be allowed to use phones for research in class. Phones can reach facts that printed books may not include. In a class trial, students using phones found answers to research questions in half the time it took students using only textbooks. Of course, any reasonable person can see that banning phones is just old fashioned thinking. Phones are powerful learning tools.

The author writes, 'any reasonable person can see that banning phones is just old fashioned thinking.' How does this sentence function in the argument?

A) It is solid evidence because it states a measured fact about phones.
B) It is a reason that logically explains why phones reach more facts.
C) It is an emotional or biased appeal, not evidence, because it pressures readers instead of proving the point.
D) It is the author's central claim that phones should be allowed.
items.answer: C) It is an emotional or biased appeal, not evidence, because it pressures readers instead of proving the point.

steps: The sentence uses loaded wording ('any reasonable person,' 'old fashioned') to pressure the reader rather than offering facts, which makes it an emotional or biased appeal, so C is correct.
A is wrong because the sentence reports no measurement or fact; the real evidence is the timed class trial.
B is wrong because it does not explain a logical link; it simply labels disagreement as outdated.
D is wrong because the central claim is that students should be allowed to use phones, not this persuasive jab.
solution.answer: C) It is an emotional or biased appeal, not evidence, because it pressures readers instead of proving the point.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Our town should ban all skateboarding in the central park. Skateboarding is dangerous and ruins the park for everyone else. Just last summer, my cousin saw a skateboarder zoom past a baby stroller, and it was absolutely terrifying. Anyone who cares about families knows skateboarders do not belong here. Some people say a separate skate area would solve the problem, but those people simply do not understand how serious this is. The truth is plain: skateboards have no place in our park.

Why is the author's central claim that skateboarding should be banned poorly supported, even though the passage sounds forceful?

A) It is well supported, because the author writes about the issue with strong, confident language.
B) It is poorly supported, because the author offers only one secondhand story and emotional or biased wording instead of facts or reasons.
C) It is poorly supported, because skateboarding is actually a healthy form of exercise.
D) It is well supported, because the author mentions that some people suggest a separate skate area.
items.answer: B) It is poorly supported, because the author offers only one secondhand story and emotional or biased wording instead of facts or reasons.

steps: To judge support, look for relevant and sufficient reasons and evidence; here the author gives a single secondhand anecdote plus loaded phrases like 'absolutely terrifying' and 'anyone who cares about families,' which is not real proof, so B is correct.
A confuses confident, forceful wording with actual support, but strong language is not evidence.
C judges the claim by outside knowledge about exercise rather than by the support the passage itself provides, which is not how we evaluate the author's argument.
D is wrong because the author only mentions the separate skate area to dismiss it rudely, which weakens the case rather than supporting it.
solution.answer: B) It is poorly supported, because the author offers only one secondhand story and emotional or biased wording instead of facts or reasons.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The school should replace its paper textbooks with tablets. Tablets hold many books at once, so students would not have to carry heavy bags. In a pilot program, students who used tablets reported less back strain, and a school survey found that 8 out of 10 students preferred reading on a screen. Tablets also save paper, which helps the environment. Critics warn that tablets can distract students and that screen time may harm reading focus, but the author writes only that 'tablets are simply the future, and the future cannot be stopped.' Switching to tablets is the right choice.

Which statement best evaluates the author's response to the critics?

A) The author fully answers the critics by giving evidence that tablets do not distract students.
B) The author answers the critics with a slogan about 'the future' instead of evidence, so that part of the argument is left unsupported.
C) The author's whole argument is unsupported, because no evidence appears anywhere in the passage.
D) The author proves the critics wrong by showing that 8 out of 10 students preferred screens.
items.answer: B) The author answers the critics with a slogan about 'the future' instead of evidence, so that part of the argument is left unsupported.

steps: The critics raise distraction and reading focus, but the author replies only with the slogan that 'the future cannot be stopped,' which is an assertion, not evidence, so that part of the argument is unsupported and B is correct.
A is wrong because the author never gives evidence about distraction; the slogan does not address it.
C overstates the problem; the passage does include real evidence elsewhere, such as the back-strain report and the survey, so the whole argument is not unsupported.
D is wrong because the survey about screen preference does not answer the worry about distraction or reading focus, so it is an irrelevant match to the critics' point.
solution.answer: B) The author answers the critics with a slogan about 'the future' instead of evidence, so that part of the argument is left unsupported.
